data.q: How many generations does the .NET Garbage Collector use by default to organize objects on the managed heap?
o: Two (Gen 0 and Gen 1)
Three (Gen 0, Gen 1, and Gen 2)
Four (Gen 0, Gen 1, Gen 2, and Gen 3)
One (Gen 0 only)
data.e: The .NET GC uses three generations: Generation 0 (short-lived objects), Generation 1 (short-lived objects that survived Gen 0), and Generation 2 (long-lived objects).

data.q: Which generation is collected most frequently by the Garbage Collector?
o: Generation 2
Generation 1
Generation 0
Large Object Heap (LOH)
data.e: Generation 0 is collected most frequently because it contains newly allocated, short-lived objects (ephemeral segment).

data.q: What is the size threshold (approximate) for an object to be allocated on the Large Object Heap (LOH) instead of the Small Object Heap (SOH)?
o: 16 KB
64 KB
85 KB
1 MB
data.e: Objects that are 85,000 bytes (approx 85 KB) or larger are allocated on the Large Object Heap (LOH).

data.q: Which interface should a class implement to release unmanaged resources deterministically?
o: ICloneable
IDisposable
IComparable
IEquatable
data.e: IDisposable provides the Dispose() method for deterministic cleanup of unmanaged resources. The GC does not call Dispose() automatically.

data.q: What is the purpose of the `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)` call inside a `Dispose()` method?
o: To force an immediate garbage collection
To promote the object to Generation 2
To prevent the finalizer from running a second time
To pin the object in memory
data.e: If Dispose() has already cleaned up unmanaged resources, calling GC.SuppressFinalize tells the GC not to call the object's finalizer (~ClassName), improving performance.

data.q: Which GC mode is optimized for applications with a user interface to minimize pause times?
o: Server GC
Workstation GC (Concurrent)
Background GC (Server)
No GC
data.e: Workstation GC with concurrent mode enabled (default for client apps) performs collections on a background thread to keep the UI responsive.

data.q: What happens during the 'Mark' phase of the Garbage Collection algorithm?
o: Memory is compacted and pointers are updated
The GC identifies all objects still reachable from roots
Finalizers are queued for execution
Memory is returned to the OS
data.e: The Mark phase traverses the object graph from GC roots (stack, statics, CPU registers) marking all reachable objects as live.

o: An object allocated on the Large Object Heap
A reference held by the finalizer thread
A storage location that the GC considers a starting point for reachability analysis (e.g., local variables, static fields)
The internal data structure managing generations
data.e: GC Roots include stack variables, static fields, CPU registers, and pinned handles. Objects reachable from roots cannot be collected.

data.q: Which method allows you to explicitly request a Garbage Collection (though generally discouraged)?
o: GC.Collect()
GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers()
GC.KeepAlive()
GC.AddMemoryPressure()
data.e: GC.Collect() forces a collection. It accepts an optional generation parameter. It is rarely needed in production code.

data.q: What is the primary difference between the Small Object Heap (SOH) and the Large Object Heap (LOH) regarding memory compaction?
o: LOH is compacted every Gen 0 collection; SOH is never compacted
SOH is compacted during collections; LOH is not compacted by default (prior to .NET 4.5.1/5.0 options)
Both are compacted simultaneously
Compaction only happens on Generation 2 collections for both
data.e: Historically, the LOH was not compacted to avoid the performance cost of moving large memory blocks. .NET 4.5.1 introduced GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode to opt-in. The SOH is compacted regularly.

o: The object from being promoted to Gen 2
The object from being allocated on the LOH
The object from being collected prematurely while a method is still using it (e.g., via an unmanaged pointer)
The finalizer from running
data.e: GC.KeepAlive creates a reference to the object until the method call, preventing the JIT/GC from optimizing away the reference and collecting the object while it is still in use by unmanaged code.

data.q: In .NET Core / .NET 5+, which GC mode is the default for Server applications (e.g., ASP.NET Core)?
o: Workstation GC (Concurrent)
Workstation GC (Non-Concurrent)
Server GC (Background)
Server GC (Non-Concurrent)
data.e: Server GC is the default for ASP.NET Core apps. It creates a heap per logical CPU and uses Background GC by default for Gen 2 collections.

data.q: What is 'Memory Pressure' in the context of the GC?
o: High CPU usage caused by the GC
A hint to the GC that unmanaged memory has been allocated, prompting it to run collections more frequently
The amount of memory used by the JIT compiler
The size of the Generation 0 budget
data.e: GC.AddMemoryPressure informs the GC about unmanaged memory allocations (e.g., via P/Invoke) so it can schedule collections appropriately, as the GC only tracks managed memory size.

data.q: Which of the following statements about Finalizers (Destructors in C#) is TRUE?
o: They run immediately when an object goes out of scope
They run on a dedicated Finalizer thread, at an indeterminate time after the object becomes unreachable
They are guaranteed to run in the order of object creation
They can safely access other managed objects that also have finalizers
data.e: Finalizers run non-deterministically on the Finalizer thread. Accessing other finalizable objects is unsafe because they may have already been finalized.

o: To prevent the object from being promoted to Gen 1
To prevent the GC from moving the object in memory (required for passing buffers to unmanaged code)
To pin the object in Generation 0 permanently
To mark the object as a GC Root
data.e: Pinned handles prevent the compacting collector from relocating the object. This is essential when passing a managed array/buffer pointer to unmanaged APIs (P/Invoke). Overuse fragments the heap.

data.q: What does the `System.GC.GetTotalMemory(bool forceFullCollection)` method return?
o: The total virtual memory reserved by the process
The number of bytes currently allocated on the managed heap
The size of the Large Object Heap only
The amount of free memory available to the OS
data.e: GetTotalMemory returns the number of bytes currently thought to be allocated on the managed heap. If forceFullCollection is true, it waits for a GC to finish before returning.
